design_detail: Natural-history follow-up of a stratified random sample (by gender, ethnicity and treatment modality) of admissions, mostly from 1996, to publicly funded Los Angeles County substance-use treatment for methamphetamine use. Monthly methamphetamine-use timelines were reconstructed retrospectively from the Natural History Interview at about 3 years after the index treatment episode (n=350) and at a second interview 2 to 4 years later (n=277). Outcome: months of continuous methamphetamine abstinence from discharge until the first month with any use. Kaplan–Meier-type survival description and a Cox proportional-hazards model with data-driven predictor selection.
can_establish: How often, and how soon, people discharged from usual-care treatment for methamphetamine use in one US county in the mid-1990s reported resuming any use, how often they later regained abstinence, and which self-reported characteristics were associated with time to first use in this sample.
cannot_establish: That any predictor causes earlier or later relapse (observational, self-selected exposures, data-driven model); in particular, the strong association with post-discharge self-help or further treatment is built into the way that variable was coded (participation before relapse, treated as a baseline characteristic), so it cannot show that continuing care prevents relapse. Nor can it show what current treatment achieves (index treatment 1996, data collected 1999 to 2003) or the effect of treatment against no treatment (no untreated comparison).

sample.recruitment: Treatment registry: admission records sampled from the California Alcohol and Drug Data System for the publicly funded Los Angeles County treatment system, mostly 1996 admissions; 62% residential and 38% outpatient index episodes (Methods › 2.1; Table 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Admissions of clients using methamphetamine to the county system; no further eligibility criteria are given in this paper (sampling details are in earlier reports from the project, which were not read).
sample.demographics: 56.3% men; 16.6% African-American, 29.7% Hispanic, 47.1% non-Hispanic White, 6.6% other or mixed; mean age at admission 29.4 (SD 6.9); 32.0% with less than high-school education; employed in 29.9% of the months in the 2 years before admission; 51.4% admitted under legal pressure; 19.1% self-reported an ever-diagnosed major mental illness; 33.1% reported sexual abuse before age 15; 56.0% reported parental alcohol or drug problems (Table 1).
sample.attrition: 75% of sampled admissions were located and 76% of those located were interviewed, so roughly 57% of the sampled records are in the analysis (editors' calculation; deaths and incomplete data are among the losses). 277 of 350 (79%) had the second interview. Those without a second interview contributed shorter histories (mean 39 versus 66 months) and were right-censored. Two missing predictor values were filled by multiple imputation (Methods › 2.1, 2.4).
sample.selection_effects: Only people who survived, could be found and agreed to be interviewed about 3 years after treatment are analysed; the authors report no differences between analysed and non-analysed admissions on the admission-record variables (education, age at first use, age at admission, prior treatment, employment, homelessness, pregnancy, legal supervision), but people who died or were not located may differ in exactly the outcome studied. The strata were sampled within gender, ethnicity and modality, and no sampling weights are mentioned, so the descriptive percentages describe the sample rather than necessarily the 1996 admission population.

exposure.measurement: Not a drug-exposure study: the 'exposures' are 17 candidate predictors, all self-reported at the Natural History Interview about 3 years after the index treatment (post-discharge self-help or further treatment from both interviews). Several are lifetime ('ever') measures recorded after the outcome period had begun: ever sold methamphetamine, ever injected, ever diagnosed with major mental illness, having experienced paranoia, hallucinations and violent behaviour attributed to methamphetamine.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Pre-treatment use: methamphetamine on a mean of 15.7 (SD 10.3) days per month in the 2 years before admission; 30.0% first used before age 16; 46.6% had ever injected drugs (Table 1). Index treatment lasted a mean of 3.7 months (SD 3.2; range 1 to 18).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed; only methamphetamine use is analysed. The predictor set includes lifetime injection of any drug; other substance use after treatment is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; abstinence is the outcome. Relapse is defined as any methamphetamine use in a month, so a single use counts; 36% are counted as relapsing in the first month, including people who were still using when they left treatment.

comparison.controls: No untreated or alternative-treatment comparison group; comparisons are between subgroups of the treated sample defined by the predictors.
comparison.matching: None. The reduced Cox model adjusts each of its five predictors for the other four only.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Motivation, self-efficacy, social networks, quality of life and clinically assessed psychiatric diagnoses were not measured, as the authors acknowledge (Discussion › 4.1); these plausibly drive both self-help participation and abstinence.

outcomes.instruments: Natural History Interview: a face-to-face life-history interview with memory aids and corroborative information, from which a monthly methamphetamine-use timeline was built from reported use frequency and changes in frequency. Outcome: months of continuous abstinence after discharge until the first month with any use; also abstinence status in months 12, 24, 36, 48 and 60 (Methods › 2.2, 2.3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Reliability checks reported in this study: 88% agreement between self-reported current or recent use and urinalysis at the first interview; differences under 0.08 in measures of association with the predictors between proximal and distal recall of the same year. There is no biological verification of the month-by-month history itself.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Relapse' is the first calendar month with any methamphetamine use after discharge; 'continuing abstinence' is its complement. No distinction is made between a single lapse and a return to regular use.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 17 candidate predictors were screened (4 dropped at p > 0.65 in univariate models, 13 entered a full model whose results are not presented, 5 retained at p < 0.20); the authors acknowledge that the several analyses raise the risk of type I error (Discussion › 4.1).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: predictors and outcome were collected in the same interviews.

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive (n=350 unless stated): relapse within 12 months of discharge 61% (editors' 95% CI about 56 to 66%), comprising 36% with no abstinent month, 14% in months 2 to 6 and 11% in months 7 to 12; relapse in year 2 7%, years 3 and 4 3% each, year 5 2%, years 6 to 7 1%; 23% abstinent throughout their observed follow-up. Continuing abstinence for at least 2, 3, 4 and 5 years: 32%, 26%, 21% and 13% of the whole sample; 32%, 32%, 26% and 23% of those followed at least that long (n=350, 325, 277, 206). At least 5 years of continuous abstinence: 47 of 350 (13%; editors' 95% CI 10 to 17%) and 47 of 206 with 5 years of follow-up (23%; 18 to 29%). Abstinent in month 12: 66%; month 24: 75%; months 36, 48, 60: 77%, 80%, 79% of those observable. Among the 206 followed 60 months: mean 44 abstinent months out of 60; the 159 who relapsed did so after a mean of 7 months, 94% of them later had at least 6 months of abstinence, and they averaged 39 abstinent months. Reduced Cox model (n=350; likelihood-ratio chi-square 106.46, df 5): parental alcohol or drug problems HR 1.35 (95% CI 1.05 to 1.73), p = 0.020; ever sold methamphetamine HR 1.48 (1.15 to 1.90), p = 0.002; all three methamphetamine-related problems (paranoia, hallucinations, violence) HR 0.75 (0.58 to 0.97), p = 0.027; each additional month in the index treatment HR 0.93 (0.89 to 0.97), p = 0.001; post-discharge self-help or other treatment before relapse HR 0.29 (0.22 to 0.39), p < 0.001. HR above 1 means earlier relapse.
analysis.covariates: The five predictors are mutually adjusted in the reduced model; demographics, education, employment, age at first use, injection, use frequency, legal pressure, age at admission and modality were screened out by p-value. No adjustment for treatment programme clustering (intraclass correlation under 0.001).
analysis.preregistration_detail: None reported; the authors state they used a model-building approach because there were no prespecified hypotheses (Methods › 2.4).
analysis.selective_reporting: The full 13-predictor model is not presented, so the reader sees only the predictors that survived p-value selection. Sensitivity analyses are described only as showing 'substantial robustness' and are in an unread supplement. Use of other substances after treatment is not reported.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 350 participants and about 270 relapse events (77%), the model has ample events for five predictors; the issue is selection and coding bias rather than precision.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In this 1996 county treatment sample, 61% reported using methamphetamine again within a year of discharge (36% within the first month), and relapse then slowed: 7% in year 2 and 2 to 3% a year afterwards. Most people who relapsed also regained abstinence: point abstinence was 66% in month 12 and about 77 to 80% in months 36 to 60, and those followed 5 years averaged 44 abstinent months out of 60. In the Cox model, post-discharge self-help or further treatment before relapse had the largest association (HR 0.29), with smaller associations for parental substance problems, selling methamphetamine, more months in treatment and self-reported methamphetamine-related psychiatric problems.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that 61% relapsed within a year and 25% during years 2 to 5, and names the predictors as protective and risk factors; the conclusion says the results support early and long-term continuing care. Gaps: (1) the Results' own year-by-year figures give 15% relapsing in years 2 to 5 (editors' calculation: 7 + 3 + 3 + 2); the abstract's 25% matches the fall in unconditional continuing abstinence from 39% to 13%, which counts people whose follow-up ended before 5 years as no longer abstinent. (2) The 'protective' self-help variable was coded as participation after discharge and before relapse but entered as a fixed baseline characteristic, so people who relapsed early had almost no time to be classified as participants; this immortal-time construction biases the hazard ratio towards protection and is not discussed. Several other predictors ('ever' sold, 'ever' diagnosed) were recorded after the outcome period began, so their timing relative to relapse is unknown. (3) The abstract omits the point-abstinence and re-abstinence results, which give a much more favourable picture of long-term course than the relapse figures alone. (4) The continuing-care recommendation is reasonable as a hypothesis but rests on these associations, not on any comparison of care.

timeline.event: Brecht, von Mayrhauser and Anglin: preliminary analysis of the first 98 interviewees from this cohort, with 57% one-year continuous abstinence and age at first use predicting relapse; neither finding held in the complete sample (Discussion, 2nd and 9th paragraphs).
Rawson et al.: status of people who used methamphetamine, 2 to 5 years after outpatient treatment (cited as an earlier long-term follow-up).
Mooney et al.: 22% three-year continuous abstinence in the Methamphetamine Treatment Project, close to this study's 26% (cited in the Discussion).
McKetin et al. (MATES, Australia): 31% one-year continuous abstinence after residential treatment, against 39% here (cited in the Discussion).
This study: the longest follow-up of continuous post-treatment methamphetamine abstinence identified by its authors (mean 60.5 months).

replication.where_it_stands: The pattern of frequent early relapse followed by repeated periods of abstinence is consistent with the shorter follow-ups the authors cite, from different countries and treatment settings. The predictor findings have not been replicated and one of them (self-help) is structurally biased; another earlier predictor from the same cohort (age at first use) did not survive in the complete sample. Data reflect 1996 usual care in one US county.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse grants R01DA11020, R01DA025113 and P30 DA016383-06 (first author); R01DA025113 (second author).
funding.declared_conflicts: Neither author declares a conflict of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors at UCLA Integrated Substance Abuse Programs (Department of Biobehavioral Sciences, David Geffen School of Medicine). The first author designed the study and did the analysis; the cohort is the authors' own long-running natural-history project.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people leaving current methamphetamine treatment, with frequent biologically verified use measurement and continuing-care participation recorded as a time-varying exposure from discharge (or, for continuing care itself, a randomized trial of continuing care against usual discharge), reporting both time to first use and point and sustained abstinence over 5 years, with deaths and incarceration tracked as competing events.

domains.note: Associations adjusted only for the other selected predictors; motivation, social support, psychiatric diagnoses and post-discharge circumstances were not measured and plausibly drive both self-help participation and abstinence.

The self-help or further-treatment variable is defined by participation before relapse but entered as a fixed covariate from discharge (immortal-time bias favouring protection). 'Ever' predictors were recorded about 3 years after discharge and may post-date relapse. All predictors are self-reported.
About 57% of sampled admissions were interviewed; no differences on admission-record variables, but people who died or were not located are missing, and stratified sampling is not weighted.
Subsequent treatment episodes, incarceration and other events that constrain use during follow-up are not modelled, apart from their partial inclusion in the self-help or further-treatment variable.
73 participants without a second interview were censored at a mean of 39 months; censoring may be informative. Only two predictor values were imputed.

Month-by-month use reconstructed by retrospective self-report over several years; reliability checks (88% agreement with urinalysis for current use; similar associations under proximal and distal recall) support but do not verify the timeline.
Predictors chosen by univariate screening (p > 0.65 dropped) and then by p < 0.20 from a full model that is not reported; sensitivity analyses are only in a supplement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: For the predictor associations, and above all the headline association with post-discharge self-help or further treatment (HR 0.29), the coding of that variable builds in a survival advantage, and selection of predictors by p-value without the full model shown makes the remaining hazard ratios optimistic. The descriptive relapse and abstinence figures are at lower risk: they depend mainly on retrospective self-report and on who could be found and interviewed, and are best read as describing survivors of a 1996 county treatment cohort.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 350 people from a stratified random sample of (mostly 1996) admissions to publicly funded Los Angeles County treatment for methamphetamine use, interviewed about 3 years after the index episode; 277 (79%) re-interviewed 2 to 4 years later. Mean post-discharge follow-up 60.5 months (SD 14.8); 93% followed at least 36 months, 80% at least 48, 59% at least 60.
61% resumed methamphetamine use within 12 months of discharge: 36% had no abstinent month after discharge, 14% relapsed in months 2 to 6 and 11% in months 7 to 12.
key_findings.note: Editors' 95% CI for 61% of 350: about 56 to 66% (Wilson). Relapse means any use in a month.

key_findings.finding: After the first year relapse slowed: 7% of the sample relapsed in year 2 (3% in months 13 to 18, 4% in months 19 to 24), 3% in each of years 3 and 4, 2% in year 5 and 1% in years 6 to 7; 77% relapsed within their observed follow-up and 23% stayed abstinent throughout (abstinence durations 22 to 90 months).

At least 5 years of continuous abstinence: 47 people, 13% of the full sample (editors' 95% CI 10 to 17%) and 23% of the 206 with at least 5 years of follow-up (18 to 29%). Continuing abstinence for at least 2, 3, 4 and 5 years was 32%, 26%, 21% and 13% of the full sample.
key_findings.note: The full-sample figures fall partly because of censoring (41% were followed less than 5 years), so they are lower bounds; the conditional figures are closer to survival estimates.

key_findings.finding: Point abstinence (no use in that month) was 66% in month 12 and 75% in month 24; among those observable, 77% in month 36, 80% in month 48 and 79% in month 60.

Among the 206 followed for 60 months, participants averaged 44 abstinent months out of 60; the 159 who relapsed did so after a mean of 7 months, 94% of them later had at least 6 months of abstinence within the 60 months, and they averaged 39 abstinent months.

Reduced Cox model (n=350): post-discharge self-help or other treatment before relapse HR 0.29 (95% CI 0.22 to 0.39), p < 0.001; each additional month in the index treatment HR 0.93 (0.89 to 0.97), p = 0.001; all three methamphetamine-related problems (paranoia, hallucinations, violent behaviour) HR 0.75 (0.58 to 0.97), p = 0.027; parental alcohol or drug problems HR 1.35 (1.05 to 1.73), p = 0.020; ever sold methamphetamine HR 1.48 (1.15 to 1.90), p = 0.002. Model chi-square 106.46 (df 5) against 110.71 (df 13) for the unreported full model.
key_findings.note: Editors' check: each hazard ratio and interval is reproduced from its printed coefficient and standard error. The self-help variable is coded as participation before relapse but treated as a baseline covariate, which biases its hazard ratio towards protection (immortal time).

key_findings.finding: 38.3% reported self-help and/or further treatment after discharge and before relapse (21% self-help only, 6% other treatment only, 11% both).

Race/ethnicity, sexual abuse before 15, self-reported major mental illness and treatment modality (residential versus outpatient) showed little univariate relation to time to relapse (p > 0.65) and were dropped; age at first use, which predicted relapse in an earlier analysis of the first 98 participants, was not retained in the complete sample.
Agreement between self-reported current or recent methamphetamine use and urinalysis at the first interview was 88%.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that 25% relapsed during years 2 to 5, whereas the Results give year-by-year relapse of 7%, 3%, 3% and 2% of the sample for years 2 to 5, which sums to 15% (editors' calculation). The 25% appears to correspond to the fall in unconditional continuing abstinence from 39% at 1 year to 13% at 5 years, which treats participants censored before 5 years as if they had relapsed.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract overstates later relapse by about 10 percentage points; claims about relapse after the first year should use the Results' year-by-year figures.

reporting_issues.issue: The conditional 3-year continuing-abstinence figure (32% of the 325 followed at least 3 years) is inconsistent with the unconditional figure for the same duration (26% of 350, about 91 people, which is 28% of 325; editors' calculation) and with the reported 3% relapse during year 3, since it equals the 2-year figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the 3-year figures is wrong; the Discussion's comparison with Mooney et al. uses the 26% figure. Claims should not cite the 32% conditional 3-year value.

reporting_issues.issue: The second interview is described as 2 to 3 years after the first in the abstract and as 2 to 4 years later in the Methods.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; follow-up duration is given precisely elsewhere (mean 60.5 months).

reporting_issues.issue: Several predictors are lifetime measures recorded at an interview about 3 years after discharge ('ever sold methamphetamine', 'ever diagnosed with major mental illness', methamphetamine-related paranoia, hallucinations and violence), and the post-discharge self-help variable is defined as participation before relapse but analysed as a fixed covariate.
reporting_issues.consequence: Temporal order between predictors and relapse is not established, and the strongest 'protective' association is inflated by design; none of this is discussed in the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The full 13-predictor model is described but its results are not presented, and the sensitivity analyses are only summarized as robust, with details in a supplement.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers cannot see the adjusted associations of the predictors that were dropped, so null findings for demographics, injection, use frequency, legal pressure and modality cannot be quantified.

reporting_issues.issue: The sample was drawn within gender, ethnicity and modality strata, but the paper does not say whether sampling was proportional or whether weights were applied.
reporting_issues.consequence: The descriptive relapse percentages may not represent the 1996 admission population of the county system.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC4550209 (NIH author manuscript; all sections, Tables 1 and 2 rendered as text, acknowledgments with funding, contributors and conflict statement, footnotes and reference list read; Figures 1 and 2 (survival curves) are images and their values were not extracted; the supplementary sensitivity analyses (a .doc file) were not read).
